source_refs.note: Exercise 1.2, Question 8 (book p. 14-15): prove four inverse hyperbolic formulas (i)-(iv); no printed answers

blocks.prompt: 8 (i) Prove the following inverse hyperbolic formula: \(\tanh^{-1} x = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right),\ x \ne 1\)
blocks.explanation:
Prove a formula for an inverse hyperbolic function, as in Examples 10 and 11.
Note the condition: \(\tanh^{-1} x\) exists only for \(|x| < 1\) (see the correction).
Plan: \(y = \tanh^{-1} x\), so \(x = \tanh y\); write with exponentials, solve for \(e^{2y}\), take \(\ln\).
steps:
Given: \(\tanh y = \frac{e^{y}-e^{-y}}{e^{y}+e^{-y}}\) takes every value in \((-1, 1)\) exactly once, so \(\tanh^{-1} x\) exists for \(|x| < 1\).
To prove: \(\tanh^{-1} x = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right)\).
Method: put \(y = \tanh^{-1} x\), so \(x = \tanh y\); solve for \(e^{2y}\); take \(\ln\).

Change the inverse into the function
\[y = \tanh^{-1} x\]
\[x = \tanh y = \dfrac{e^{y} - e^{-y}}{e^{y} + e^{-y}}\]
Why: definition of the inverse and of \(\tanh\).

Multiply top and bottom by \(e^{y}\)
\[x = \dfrac{e^{2y} - 1}{e^{2y} + 1}\]
Why: \(e^{y} \cdot e^{-y} = 1\); now only \(e^{2y}\) appears.

Solve for \(e^{2y}\)
\[xe^{2y} + x = e^{2y} - 1\]
\[1 + x = e^{2y} - xe^{2y}\]
\[1 + x = e^{2y}(1 - x)\]
\[e^{2y} = \dfrac{1+x}{1-x}\]
Why: cross-multiply, collect the \(e^{2y}\) terms on one side, take \(e^{2y}\) common, and divide by \(1 - x \ne 0\).

Take ln
\[2y = \ln\left(\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}\right)\]
\[y = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\dfrac{1+x}{1-x}\right)\]
Why: for \(-1 < x < 1\) both \(1 + x\) and \(1 - x\) are positive, so the fraction is positive and its \(\ln\) exists.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The condition is printed as \(x \ne 1\). That is not enough: \(\tanh y\) always lies in \((-1, 1)\), so \(\tanh^{-1} x\) exists only for \(|x| < 1\); for \(x > 1\) or \(x \le -1\) the fraction \(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\) is negative or zero and its \(\ln\) is not defined. The correct statement is \(\tanh^{-1} x = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right)\), \(|x| < 1\) (as in the 1.5.3 table).

blocks.prompt: 8 (ii) Prove the following inverse hyperbolic formula: \(\coth^{-1} x = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right),\ x \ne 1\)
blocks.explanation:
The printed formula is that of \(\tanh^{-1}\) and cannot hold for \(\coth^{-1}\) (see the correction); we prove the correct one.
\(\coth^{-1} x\) exists for \(|x| > 1\).
Plan: \(x = \coth y\), solve for \(e^{2y}\), take \(\ln\).
steps:
Given: \(\coth y = \frac{e^{y}+e^{-y}}{e^{y}-e^{-y}}\) (\(y \ne 0\)) takes every value with \(|x| > 1\) exactly once, so \(\coth^{-1} x\) exists for \(|x| > 1\).
To prove: the correct formula \(\coth^{-1} x = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left(\frac{x+1}{x-1}\right)\), \(|x| > 1\) (see the correction below).
Method: as in part (i): \(x = \coth y\), solve for \(e^{2y}\), take \(\ln\).

Change the inverse into the function
\[y = \coth^{-1} x\]
\[x = \coth y = \dfrac{e^{y} + e^{-y}}{e^{y} - e^{-y}}\]
\[x = \dfrac{e^{2y} + 1}{e^{2y} - 1}\]
Why: definition of \(\coth\); then multiply top and bottom by \(e^{y}\).

Solve for \(e^{2y}\)
\[xe^{2y} - x = e^{2y} + 1\]
\[xe^{2y} - e^{2y} = x + 1\]
\[e^{2y}(x - 1) = x + 1\]
\[e^{2y} = \dfrac{x+1}{x-1}\]
Why: cross-multiply, collect the \(e^{2y}\) terms, take it common, divide by \(x - 1 \ne 0\).

Take ln
\[2y = \ln\left(\dfrac{x+1}{x-1}\right)\]
\[y = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\dfrac{x+1}{x-1}\right)\]
Why: if \(x > 1\), both \(x + 1\) and \(x - 1\) are positive; if \(x < -1\), both are negative. In either case the fraction is positive, so the \(\ln\) exists.

Check: \(x = \frac{5}{3}\): \(\frac{8/3}{2/3} = 4\), so \(y = \frac{1}{2}\ln 4 = \ln 2\).
\[\coth(\ln 2) = \dfrac{2 + \frac{1}{2}}{2 - \frac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{5}{3}\]
It returns \(x\). (The printed formula at \(x = \frac{5}{3}\) would need \(\ln\left(\frac{8/3}{-2/3}\right) = \ln(-4)\), which does not exist.)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints \(\coth^{-1} x = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right),\ x \ne 1\), which is the formula of \(\tanh^{-1} x\) from part (i). It cannot be right: \(\coth^{-1} x\) exists only for \(|x| > 1\), and for every such \(x\) the fraction \(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\) is negative, so its \(\ln\) is undefined (for example \(x = 2\) gives \(\frac{3}{-1} = -3\)). The correct formula, also given in the book's own 1.5.3 table, is \(\coth^{-1} x = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left(\frac{x+1}{x-1}\right),\ |x| > 1\). That is what is proved above.

blocks.prompt: 8 (iii) Prove the following inverse hyperbolic formula: \(\operatorname{sech}^{-1} x = \ln\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}{x}\right),\ x \ne 0\)
blocks.explanation:
Prove the formula for \(\operatorname{sech}^{-1} x\). Like \(\cosh\), \(\operatorname{sech}\) is even, so its inverse uses \(y \ge 0\) and exists for \(0 < x \le 1\).
Plan: quadratic in \(e^{y}\), then choose the root with \(y \ge 0\).
steps:
Given: \(\operatorname{sech} y = \frac{2}{e^{y}+e^{-y}}\) is even, so (as for \(\cosh\)) we use only \(y \ge 0\); there it takes every value in \((0, 1]\) once. So \(\operatorname{sech}^{-1} x\) exists for \(0 < x \le 1\), with \(y \ge 0\).
To prove: \(\operatorname{sech}^{-1} x = \ln\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}{x}\right)\).
Method: \(x = \operatorname{sech} y\) gives a quadratic in \(e^{y}\); the condition \(y \ge 0\) chooses the root (as in Example 11).

Change the inverse into the function
\[y = \operatorname{sech}^{-1} x,\quad y \ge 0\]
\[x = \operatorname{sech} y = \dfrac{2}{e^{y} + e^{-y}}\]
Why: definition of the inverse on the restricted domain \(y \ge 0\).

Make a quadratic in \(e^{y}\)
\[xe^{y} + xe^{-y} = 2\]
\[xe^{2y} + x = 2e^{y}\]
\[x(e^{y})^{2} - 2e^{y} + x = 0\]
Why: cross-multiply, then multiply by \(e^{y}\). Here \(a = x\), \(b = -2\), \(c = x\).

Quadratic formula
\[e^{y} = \dfrac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 - 4x^{2}}}{2x}\]
\[= \dfrac{1 \pm \sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}{x}\]
Why: \(\sqrt{4 - 4x^{2}} = 2\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}\), real because \(0 < x \le 1\).

Choose the sign
The two roots multiply to
\[\dfrac{1 - (1 - x^{2})}{x^{2}} = 1\]
For \(0 < x < 1\) the plus root is \(> \frac{1}{x} > 1\), so the minus root lies between 0 and 1 and would give \(y = \ln(\text{minus root}) < 0\). Since \(y \ge 0\), we take the plus sign. (At \(x = 1\) both roots equal 1.)
Why: the same reasoning as Example 11.

Take ln
\[e^{y} = \dfrac{1 + \sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}{x}\]
\[\operatorname{sech}^{-1} x = \ln\left(\dfrac{1+\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}{x}\right)\]
Why: \(\ln\) undoes \(e\).

Check: \(x = \frac{4}{5}\): \(\sqrt{1 - \frac{16}{25}} = \frac{3}{5}\), so \(\frac{1 + 3/5}{4/5} = 2\) and \(y = \ln 2\).
\[\operatorname{sech}(\ln 2) = \dfrac{2}{2 + \frac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{4}{5}\]
It returns \(x\). Also \(x = 1\) gives \(\ln 1 = 0\), and \(\operatorname{sech} 0 = 1\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The condition is printed as \(x \ne 0\). That is not enough: \(\operatorname{sech} y\) takes values only in \((0, 1]\), so \(\operatorname{sech}^{-1} x\) exists only for \(0 < x \le 1\). For \(x > 1\) the root \(\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\) is not real, and for \(x < 0\) the fraction is negative, so the \(\ln\) is undefined. The correct condition is \(0 < x \le 1\) (as in the 1.5.3 table).

blocks.prompt: 8 (iv) Prove the following inverse hyperbolic formula: \(\operatorname{csch}^{-1} x = \ln\left(\frac{1}{x} + \sqrt{\frac{1}{x^{2}}+1}\right),\ x \ne 0\)
blocks.explanation:
Prove the formula for \(\operatorname{csch}^{-1} x\), defined for all \(x \ne 0\) (printed correctly).
Plan: quadratic in \(e^{y}\), then reject the negative root because \(e^{y} > 0\).
steps:
Given: \(\operatorname{csch} y =  rac{2}{e^{y}-e^{-y}}\) (\(y 
e 0\)) is one-to-one and takes every non-zero value, so \(\operatorname{csch}^{-1} x\) exists for every \(x 
e 0\).
To prove: \(\operatorname{csch}^{-1} x = \ln\left( rac{1}{x} + \sqrt{ rac{1}{x^{2}}+1}ight)\), \(x 
e 0\).
Method: \(x = \operatorname{csch} y\) gives a quadratic in \(e^{y}\); \(e^{y} > 0\) chooses the root (as in Example 10).

Change the inverse into the function
\[y = \operatorname{csch}^{-1} x\]
\[x = \operatorname{csch} y = \dfrac{2}{e^{y} - e^{-y}}\]
Why: definition of the inverse and of \(\operatorname{csch}\).

Make a quadratic in \(e^{y}\)
\[e^{y} - e^{-y} = \dfrac{2}{x}\]
\[e^{2y} - 1 = \dfrac{2}{x}e^{y}\]
\[(e^{y})^{2} - \dfrac{2}{x}e^{y} - 1 = 0\]
Why: cross-multiply, then multiply by \(e^{y}\). Here \(a = 1\), \(b = -\frac{2}{x}\), \(c = -1\).

Quadratic formula
\[e^{y} = \dfrac{\frac{2}{x} \pm \sqrt{\frac{4}{x^{2}} + 4}}{2}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{x} \pm \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{x^{2}} + 1}\]
Why: \(\sqrt{\frac{4}{x^{2}} + 4} = 2\sqrt{\frac{1}{x^{2}} + 1}\); the 2 cancels.

Choose the sign
\[\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{x^{2}} + 1} > \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}} = \left|\dfrac{1}{x}\right| \ge \dfrac{1}{x}\]
So the minus root \(\frac{1}{x} - \sqrt{\frac{1}{x^{2}}+1}\) is negative, but \(e^{y} > 0\). Take the plus sign.
Why: the same reasoning as Example 10.

Take ln
\[\operatorname{csch}^{-1} x = \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{x} + \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}+1}\right)\]
Why: \(\ln\) undoes \(e\); the plus root is positive, so the \(\ln\) exists for every \(x \ne 0\).

Check: \(x = \frac{3}{4}\): \(\frac{1}{x} = \frac{4}{3}\), \(\sqrt{\frac{16}{9} + 1} = \frac{5}{3}\), so \(y = \ln 3\).
\[\operatorname{csch}(\ln 3) = \dfrac{2}{3 - \frac{1}{3}} = \dfrac{3}{4}\]
It returns \(x\). For \(x = -\frac{3}{4}\): \(\ln\left(-\frac{4}{3} + \frac{5}{3}\right) = \ln\frac{1}{3} = -\ln 3\), and \(\operatorname{csch}(-\ln 3) = -\frac{3}{4}\).
